newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Top Chechen propagandist tries longshot bid for power.
newsitem.headline: Top Chechen propagandist tries longshot bid for power.

text.p: Armed with a single satellite telephone and working from mountain hideouts, Movladi Udugov was in some ways as powerful a weapon in Chechnya's war against Russian troops as its gritty guerrilla fighters.

As the rebel republic's wartime information minister, the wily, slightly built Udugov defeated Russia's propaganda machine with his version of events. He was not always accurate, but he repeatedly beat Moscow to the punch.
Now, with the war over, the 34-year-old is seeking the presidency of his unrecognised state in Monday's elections.

Considered one of the top four candidates in a field of sixteen, he is nonetheless a longshot whose best hope would be to force a second round against front runner Aslan Maskhadov or field commander Shamil Basayev.
Udugov has run by far the most professional campaign of any of the candidates. His flashy posters, carrying his "Islamic Order" mantra in green and red, have nearly drowned out others.

While most Chechen political TV commercials look like they were shot on cheap video cameras by honeymooning couples, his are well made and edited and show him addressing rallies, hugging children, and praying in a mosque.
Inspirational Islamic music hums in the background.
"If Russia admits that we were able to beat it in the propaganda war, then certainly it shouldn't be that hard to organise a campaign in little Chechnya," Udugov joked with reporters this week.

Hypnotically hammering away at the "Islamic Order" theme in hour-long television addresses, he expounds his philosophy on how to rebuild Chechnya's war-torn economy by setting up an Islamic bank for reconstruction and interest payments on loans.
"There will only be order in our nation when it submits to to order, Islamic order. Western civilisation is bankrupt. All it can offer is pornographic films and drug addicts," he told a recent rally.
Udugov also says he knows how to force Russia to pay what Chechnya says is $150 billion owed it in war reparations for the devastation of the war.
He points to his traditional lifestyle in the last line of his political programme.
"Married. Has two wives and four children!" it reads.
With two spouses, Tabarik and Mariam, Udugov is the only major presidential candidate to practice polygamy as allowed by Moslem custom.

His detractors say his sudden embrace of Islamic ideas is political opportunism. Fellow candidate Shamil Basayev has accused him of receiving money from radical Moslem sects in Saudi Arabia to finance his campaign, but he denies this.
